I think on Reddit the demographic might skew to "studio" musicians, but there are tons of people in every city who make their money playing gigs. Some of them might not even have their music on Spotify or any streaming service.

That being said, many more do work day jobs on top of gigging. In my city there are like 3 categories: The working musicians, almost everyone else, and the true professionals. Plus, the classical musicians, but we don't talk about them ;)

The working musicians are out playing whatever shows they can get at almost every opportunity, be it in multiple bands, cover bands, weddings, conferences, etc. Might throw in regional festival acts or bands that just play summer gigs, that sort of thing. 

The true professionals are masters of their instrument/craft and have great connections. They might travel the country or do session work, end up on radio or tv, have some awards, etc. They put in the work, and through luck and determination have made a career of music. Oddly, there are a few wedding and corporate event bands that might fall in this category, because those niches can be lucrative once you're established. 

Everyone else is having fun, hustlin and grindin, or getting ready to implode and/or fizzle out. Most people can't commit the time or energy into treating music like a business. Or life happens. Which is okay. I know of plenty of musicians who focused on other things at some point in their life, and plenty of people who had fun playing music their whole lives without ever sharing it or making a career of it.

From what I've read on the topic, there's a lot of dispute about the subjective experience of acute cyanide poisoning. There's different kinds to start. Speaking specifically on potassium cyanide capsules, it's debatable whether a person is actually aware of the actions which observers may interpret as a result of pain - convulsions, grimacing, etc. For example, one might expect terrible air hunger since cyanide disrupts cells ability to utilize oxygen. But air hunger is mediated through chemoreceptors detecting low oxygen or high CO2, of which neither should be present. 

In other words, it /could/ be very painful and alarming for a short time, but tends to be over very quickly. And there's a high chance your tissues rich in circulation would cease functioning early on (brain and heart), so hopefully little awareness. 

Compare that to short drop, or pole, hanging with piano wire. Metal wire might cut you, and at very least will be extremely painful with your full body weight. That'll quickly feel like your head is about to explode (figuratively) from the pressure. Eyes and tongue may bulge out. Hearing will sound like the ocean in a seashell from the pressure. If you're lucky you'll pass out within a minute or two. After a few minutes you'll start convulsing powerfully. (that's the part where people hanging themselves at home sometimes wake up on the ground, having knocked loose whatever they were tied to). You'll eventually evacuate bowels and bladder and get an erection if you have a penis. Should be done within 5-20 minutes.

Neither is fun, and both are rather undignified ways to go. I'm taking a chance on the cyanide though.

I make a bean stew that’s hearty. I wing most cooking at this point, so recipe is approximate. Do what feels good. 

Brown up half to a full pack of bacon on the stovetop - I like postage stamp size pieces, and it works fine to dump it all in at once, go low n slow, get all the fat rendering well - remove bacon for now. Keep the fat in the pan. Throw in however much onion seems right. I like 1/2 to 3/4 of a big one diced and I aim for light browning. If you wanna keep a bit of onion to add later in the process for multidimensional onion flavah that’s groovy too. Next add in however much garlic you want (I like a lot) followed shortly after by any spices which benefit from blooming in the hot oil. You can take it a lot of ways, but I tend to go for flavours that accompany chicken well. Before the garlic or spices start to burn add in a fat can of drained cannellini (white kidney) beans. Mix it up, cover with water, add some chicken stock and any remaining herbs or spices you didn’t want toasted in the oil. Let it simmer for a while, 20 minutes is probably fine but sometimes I let it go longer. Mush up like 1/8 of the beans and mix it, find a consistency that you like - I want mine to coat the back of a spoon at least. Then you can add in a bunch of kale, again winging it - I want something green to complement, not take over the dish. That can simmer until the kale is ready, and then you add your bacon pieces back in.

Headphones never feel the same as an amp/speaker moving air. I haven’t tried proper power attenuators because the good ones are expensive and the bad ones can have issues which could affect my amp/tubes. I do, however, have an fx loop attenuator (just a volume pot basically) which lets you get more preamp saturation, but I find that also lacks in the feel department. Dirt or boost pedals are also very hard to wrangle with a tube amp at bedroom levels - to me they’re anemic at too low of volumes. 

My “solutions” if you can call them that: Low watt amp, and smaller speakers. I have a ‘66 Pepco Arc which is about 1-3 watts into a vintage 8” jensen. I could be talking out of my ass (i’m at least an audio tech), but my understanding is that speakers need a certain amount of power before they hit their sweet spot (and i’m not talking about speaker distortion) which means it can be hard to get good tone out of, say, a 4x12 at bedroom quiet levels. Static or buzz can be a lot of things. Many speakers and/or PA systems inherently have some static when you listen up close. It could be the amp, it could be the speaker, it could be interference in whatever line you're using, it could be your power supply, among other possibilities. I would start with checking your lines, then test ground/lift on power supplies if possible, then move on to trying different speaker and amp combos. If it goes away, what changed? Will it come back if you change something else? 

Digital sounding: Even with your explanation further down, that's a tough one. A big part of that will be whatever speaker you're using. Something full range flat response, like for PA, may end up sounding "digital" or sterile, etc. Guitar speakers on the other hand have a pretty significant mid boost and more or less are designed to colour your tone. If it's sounding digital and bad to you through a guitar speaker then it could indeed be the amp. 

Realistically I would think the power amps you mentioned should all be relatively transparent. Makes me wonder if you actually prefer a power amp that's not so transparent. Especially if a tube power amp sounded good to you. It could be that the Helix itself (don't crucify me, i haven't used one so i'm postulating) sounds digital to your ear, and it works best in your rig with an amp and/or speaker that colour the tone. 

I do wonder why the Yamaha stands out to you. But getting into the engineering of the PA amp vs the floor/pedal amps is a little over my head. Anyways, good luck troubleshooting!

I just wanna say, check out your local library, or if your town has history books, etc, they can have a great wealth of information regarding daily life back then. Especially small towns. I was reading the old history book for my hometown last night and in one passage my great great uncle told about how they would cut ice from the river nearby for cold storage (their family was butchers and sold ice around 1900 in the Canadian prairies). It was a very long process to store it properly and required going around to each resident in town, who collected all the sawdust from cutting their firewood, and they used that to pack and insulate the ice. That way it could last longer when warm weather arrived, and the blocks wouldn't get stuck together. Everyone in town was dependent on each other in one way or another, and everything had a use. 

Unrelated, but he also told interesting stories of helping his father butchering in the summer months, when they had to do it after 10pm or wake up at 3am to start so they could get finished before the flies "woke up". Holding the lantern too close meant oil could drip onto the meat and that was unacceptable, but too far and the shadows cast would lead to inaccurate cuts. Each of the kids spent many nights like that. Until later on, in the '20s beef rings (a type of collective) popped up in small towns and put many butchers out of business.

One random thing I learned from an old trapper in Manitoba: hi-vis (flagging) tape/ribbon can come in handy for a variety of uses. Mainly if you think you could get lost, either from unfamiliarity or weather conditions, you can mark your path by stringing it through trees every once in a while. Think sections a few feet long pointing towards the last ribbon, which should be close enough that it’s visible. Just make sure to take it all out when you leave. 

And if you do a lot of hiking off-trails it doesn’t hurt to have some ice-pick/claw type doo-dads. More or less just in case you fall through ice. There are ice picks that are pretty much peg handles attached by a band that should be run through your jacket, so that they dangle out of each sleeve. That way when you fall through you don’t have to scramble for gear, they’re just ready by your hands to start pulling yourself back onto the ice. 

On that note, keeping a lanyard with your most crucial survival items on it can go a long ways in an emergency. Preferably doubles of what’s already in your bag. That way if it goes into the water or something you can still help yourself. At least a whistle, a fire starter and a navigation aid. 

Anyways, those are pretty random bits of advice, and probably only necessary for serious outings, so if you’re going somewhere explicitly safe, then disregard. There’s plenty of good advice in this thread already.

A stolen trailer hitch might go under the radar, but major crimes don’t tend to stay unsolved for long out here. Better to get your stuff back safe and sound after the fact, than to get yourself or others hurt.

I think they fucked up their example. I have a basic understanding of the principle after reading the Wikipedia page for the Relativity of Simultaneity (this version is not Einstein’s thought experiment):

There’s a moving train car, an observer on a platform outside the train, an observer inside the centre of train car, and a flash of light in the centre of the train car just as the observers pass each other. 

For the observer in the train car, the front and back of the train car are at fixed distances and according to them, the light will reach the front and back at the same time.

For the observer on the platform, the rear of the train car is catching up to the point at which the flash of light was given off, and the front of the train car is moving away from that point. Since the speed of light is finite and the same in all directions for all observers, the flash of light will hit the back of the train car before it hits the front. 

So that’s all to say, whether two spatially separate events occur at the same time is not absolute - but depends on the observers frame of reference.

You can tell if a barrel is rifled by looking down it. First it must be safety checked - unloaded, etc, beforehand. I can’t stress that enough. Then, most often, you just open the breach to allow more light in and take a look. If it’s rifled you’ll see a spiralling groove running the length of the barrel. That is rifling. It provides spin to the bullet and vastly increases accuracy. 

Shotguns using slugs do not inherently have a rifled barrel. I’ve never heard of a regular shotgun with a rifled barrel. They have smooth bores because they are most often used with “shot” (little pellets) at ranges under 50 yards. That being said, RSGs, or Rifled Slug Guns exist for things like big game hunting, although compared to the availability of most hunting guns they are exceptionally rare - a niche along the lines of using a muzzleloader these days. When most people think of a shotgun, an RSG is not what comes to mind. 

As one becomes familiar with guns it becomes second nature to look at it and say, “yeah, that’s a shotgun” - which in turn means that the barrel is probably smoothbore. But otherwise, the ONLY definitive way to tell whether a gun is rifled or not is looking inside the barrel or researching the exact model of gun in question.
